row.basis: sun as runner on its course
row.note: The commentary extends 87:1's galloping-horse image to stars swimming in their courses; this psalm depicts the sun rejoicing like a champion to run its course, adding a celestial runner.
The commentary joins 87:3's guidance to the later place in the procession; the psalm says God guides the speaker and afterward receives him to glory, making guidance lead toward a later reward.
The commentary turns 87:3's guidance into vanguard leaders; Exodus says YHWH goes before Israel in cloud and fire to lead the route, giving guidance a literal front-of-column position.

row.basis: cloud shifts from front to rear
row.note: The commentary tracks leaders and those at the people's rear; as Egypt approaches, Exodus moves the divine messenger and cloud from before Israel to behind them, making the procession's order protective.
The commentary says the group's “after” names those at its end; Numbers assigns Dan's camp the rear guard for Israel's moving camps, a concrete final rank in the column.
The commentary develops a front rank and followers behind; Joshua's Jericho procession places armed men before the priests and a rear guard behind the ark, adding a ritual march with both positions.
The commentary maps first and last onto a moving line; Isaiah describes the departing people going without haste because YHWH goes before them and Israel's God is their rear guard.

The commentary sets a leading rank against those at the rear; Isaiah promises healing with righteousness going before the people and YHWH's glory as their rear guard, giving the order a salvific meaning.

The commentary brings together swimming water and a running horse; Habakkuk's theophany has God tread the sea with horses, a concrete meeting of water and equine movement without equating their actions.

row.basis: people led through depths like a sure-footed horse
row.note: The commentary praises an animal's well-placed steps and recalls swimming; Isaiah describes God leading Israel through depths like a horse in the wilderness that does not stumble, joining deep-water passage to sure-footed motion.
The commentary's yusr gloss depicts an animal transferring its legs well; the psalm says God makes the speaker's feet like a deer and sets him on high places, making sure-footed ascent a divine gift.

The commentary reads 87:8's animal stride as well-placed movement; Habakkuk's prayer gives the speaker hind-like feet on high places amid crop failure and distress, adding sure footing as trust through crisis.

row.basis: running with horses as endurance test
row.note: The commentary says the trailing horse has saved some running for later; Jeremiah's rebuke asks whether the prophet can contend with horses if footmen tire him, making endurance rather than an early lead the test.

The commentary says the first to arrive is not necessarily the winner; Ecclesiastes says the race is not to the swift and outcomes do not reliably follow strength or speed, directly unsettling rank by pace.
The commentary distinguishes the first horse from the one following; Ahimaaz outruns the Cushite in a messenger race, supplying a narrative pair of first and trailing runners.

row.basis: first arrival lacks the decisive answer
row.note: The commentary warns that the first to arrive need not win; after outrunning the Cushite, Ahimaaz reaches David but cannot say what happened to Absalom, so speed does not deliver the needed result.

The commentary says the one behind may matter more than the first; the Cushite arrives after Ahimaaz and answers David about Absalom, completing a messenger race in which the later report is decisive.

row.basis: horses set against invoking God's name
row.note: The commentary pairs 87:15's remembering the Lord's name with horse imagery; this psalm contrasts trust in horses with invoking YHWH's name, adding a counterpoint in which the horse is inadequate as security.
The commentary couples guidance with an animal's ordered stride; the psalmist says he will run the way of God's commandments when his heart is enlarged, turning directed movement into obedience.
The commentary's horse saves part of its run for the later stretch; Isaiah promises that those who hope in YHWH will run without weariness, making sustained movement the result of renewed strength.

row.basis: Arabic source root س ب ح and Aramaic š-b-ḥ, praise
row.note: The commentary labels 87:1's Arabic root س ب ح and develops swimming and galloping associations; Daniel's Aramaic prayer uses the cognate root š-b-ḥ to praise God, grounding the worship sense without importing Daniel's word into the motion gloss.

row.basis: Arabic source root ص ل و and Aramaic ṣ-l-y, pray
row.note: The commentary labels 87:15 فَصَلَّى as prayer, then notes a second-horse sense in its lexical family; Daniel's Aramaic cognate describes his three daily prayers, anchoring the worship sense while leaving the horse image secondary.

row.basis: Arabic source آخرة and Hebrew אחרית, latter end
row.note: The commentary says the Arabic “after/latter” root names those at the rear; Ecclesiastes uses the Hebrew cognate אחרית for a matter's end, and explicitly calls that end better than its beginning.
The commentary says the later runner may be better than the first arrival; Ecclesiastes explicitly values a matter's end over its beginning, giving the temporal reversal a wisdom saying.

row.basis: vestibule before the World to Come
row.note: The commentary makes the nearer life the first part of a sequence and the afterlife the later part; Avot pictures this world as a vestibule before the World to Come, adding a preparatory threshold image.

row.basis: relative worth of the two worlds
row.note: The commentary calls the later life better and more enduring; Avot preserves both valuations: an hour of good deeds here exceeds the future world's whole life, yet an hour of its bliss exceeds all this world's life, complicating a simple ranking.

row.basis: fruit now, principal preserved for the World to Come
row.note: The commentary contrasts the near life with what remains afterward; Peah says some deeds bear fruit in this world while their principal remains for the World to Come, adding a specific image of reward held for later.

The commentary says the later life is more enduring than the present; Wisdom says the righteous dead seem destroyed to observers but have hope full of immortality, adding the hidden outcome behind apparent loss.

The commentary criticizes preferring the nearer life over what follows; the second Maccabean martyr refuses the king's offer and expects the King of the universe to raise him, presenting the contrary choice of future life over present survival.
The commentary calls the hereafter better and lasting; a brother facing execution says the dead will be raised to life, adding resurrection as the concrete future that makes present death bearable.

The commentary distinguishes the leading and following horses and says early arrival is not the whole contest; Paul invokes runners in a stadium and urges the Corinthians to run to obtain the prize, making disciplined pursuit—not mere rank—the point.

The commentary calls the later life more enduring and compares it to a horse saving its run; Paul contrasts athletes' perishable wreath with the imperishable one sought by Christians, joining race discipline to lasting reward.

row.basis: run the set race with endurance
row.note: The commentary's final runner preserves strength for the later stretch; Hebrews tells its hearers to run the race set before them with endurance, making perseverance the necessary path to the finish.

row.basis: joy set ahead of present suffering
row.note: The commentary values what comes later over the first arrival; Hebrews says Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him and then sat at God's right hand, giving present suffering a future-directed end.

The commentary's race image turns the two lives into first and later positions; Paul says he forgets what lies behind and reaches toward what lies ahead, making forward orientation the posture of pursuit.
The commentary says the later result is better than the early lead; Paul presses toward the goal for the prize of God's upward call in Christ, specifying a future prize as the runner's measure.
The commentary warns that arriving first is not the final victory; Paul says near death that he has finished the race and kept the faith, making completion rather than an early position decisive.

row.basis: crown laid up for that day
row.note: The commentary says the latter life is better and longer-lasting; Paul expects a crown of righteousness reserved for the Lord's appearing, giving the race a reward kept for the end.
The commentary says people prefer the life of this world; John warns against loving the world and its desires, giving a direct ethical reversal of that preference.

row.basis: world passes, God's will remains forever
row.note: The commentary calls the hereafter better and more enduring; John says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, stating transience versus permanence.
The commentary says people prefer the nearer life despite what follows; Jesus warns that earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth and corrosion, adding a concrete form of what does not last.
The commentary calls what follows more enduring than the present; Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy, specifying a lasting object of preference.

row.basis: gain the world, lose one's life
row.note: The commentary criticizes preferring worldly life over the better later outcome; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world yet forfeit one's life, making the choice a question of ultimate value.

The commentary sets present life against a better later one; Jesus promises those who leave home or kin for his name a hundredfold and eternal life in the age to come, making present relinquishment point forward.
The commentary says the early arrival is not necessarily the winner; after the promise of eternal life, Jesus says many who are first will be last and last first, explicitly reversing expected order.

row.basis: late workers paid before the first
row.note: The commentary makes the first arrival no guarantee of winning; in the vineyard parable's conclusion the last are first and first last, adding a narrative reversal of rank and reward.

row.basis: rich toward God rather than stored wealth
row.note: The commentary says people prefer the life now at the expense of what follows; Jesus ends the rich fool's story by contrasting treasure for oneself with being rich toward God, adding a sudden-death case of misplaced priority.

The commentary says the first life is not the final winner and the later one is better; Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but now Lazarus is comforted and he is in agony.

row.basis: departing to Christ is far better
row.note: The commentary says the afterlife is better than the current life; Paul says he desires to depart and be with Christ because that is far better, while remaining in the flesh benefits others.

row.basis: present suffering outweighed by coming glory
row.note: The commentary compares the present life with a better and more lasting later one; Paul says present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed, making the future outweigh the present.
The commentary contrasts the near world with what lasts afterward; Paul says visible things are temporary and unseen things eternal, giving the present/later contrast an explicit duration.

row.basis: preferring to be with the Lord
row.note: The commentary says the later life is better than the present one; Paul says he would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord, making the preference explicit while describing his own hope.

row.basis: sun's ordered course through the gates
row.note: The commentary's source gloss pictures stars swimming in their courses; the Astronomical Book lays out the sun's recurring course through the heavenly gates, adding a Jewish account of ordered celestial motion without equating it with swimming.

The commentary gives the stars an ordered orbit; Enoch's vision associates a sinful age with celestial lights departing their appointed order, preserving a contrary image in which the course itself fails.

row.basis: water deep enough to swim in
row.note: The commentary gives س ب ح the literal gloss “swim in water”; Ezekiel's temple river grows until it is deep enough for swimming, adding a sacred, measured current as a concrete water-motion image.
The commentary's yusr gloss praises an animal's well-transferred steps; Proverbs calls several creatures stately in their going, making dignified gait itself the point rather than speed.

row.basis: separated herds in a moving caravan
row.note: The commentary arranges horses and camels by those ahead and behind; Jacob sends successive animal droves ahead with space between them, adding a staged caravan whose order serves a plan.

row.basis: Arabic source root ء خ ر and Hebrew אחרית, latter end
row.note: The commentary labels 87:17's Arabic al-ākhirah with the root ء خ ر and describes what remains behind; Moses recalls wilderness testing intended to do Israel good at its אחרית, its latter end, giving the cognate a delayed-benefit context.

row.basis: Arabic source root ء خ ر and Hebrew אחור, behind
row.note: The commentary uses the Arabic root for both the afterlife and those at the rear; the psalm says God encompasses the speaker “behind and before,” showing the Hebrew cognate's spatial sense alongside the source's temporal one.

row.basis: Arabic source al-ākhirah and Hebrew אחרית, future
row.note: The commentary says the Arabic “after/latter” names those at a group's end; the psalm uses Hebrew אחרית for the peaceful person's future, adding an ethical outcome to the cognate's temporal sense.

The commentary contrasts the near life with what lasts afterward; the final brother says those who endured brief suffering have entered ever-flowing life, making the short/lasting contrast explicit in a martyr's speech.
The commentary says the later life is better and more enduring; Daniel describes sleepers in the dust awakening, some to everlasting life, supplying an explicit resurrection horizon.

row.basis: rest, then rise at the end of days
row.note: The commentary makes the afterlife the latter stage and calls it lasting; Daniel is told to go to his rest and rise for his allotted inheritance at the end of days, giving that sequence a personal resurrection outcome.
The commentary says the message is in earlier scrolls and names Moses; Deuteronomy says Moses finishes writing the words of the Torah in a book, a concrete Mosaic witness to written scripture.

row.basis: book of the law deposited as witness
row.note: The commentary names Moses among the sources of the earlier scrolls; Moses orders the written book of the law placed beside the covenant ark as a witness, adding its preserved public role.

The commentary extends a race's front and rear positions to the afterlife; Berakhot portrays the World to Come without eating, trade, jealousy, hatred, or competition, with the righteous enjoying God's presence, limiting the race image to this life's sequence.

row.basis: thanksgiving and calling on God's name
row.note: The commentary says the worshipper remembers the Lord's name and prays; the psalm joins a thanksgiving offering with calling on YHWH's name, adding a concrete liturgical form of that pairing.

row.basis: the present age and the future age
row.note: The commentary contrasts the near life with the better, lasting life after it; in chapter 7 Uriel compares the hard passage of the present age with the future age's reward. Verse divisions vary by edition, so this is cited at chapter level.
The commentary condemns preferring the near life over what follows; Esau trades his birthright for food and despises it, a concrete choice of immediate satisfaction over a later inheritance.

row.basis: Esau sells inheritance for a meal
row.note: The commentary's 87:16–17 contrast is immediate preference against later good; Hebrews names Esau as one who sold his birthright for a single meal, turning the Genesis episode into an ethical warning about short-term choice.

row.basis: later regret cannot recover the blessing
row.note: The commentary says the early choice may not win the final outcome; Hebrews recalls that Esau later sought the blessing with tears but could not reverse what happened, adding the consequence of a short-sighted exchange.

row.basis: Abraham's company desires a better country
row.note: The commentary names Abraham in the former scrolls and says the later life is better; Hebrews says the patriarchs desired a better, heavenly country, making Abrahamic faith look beyond the present homeland.
The commentary criticizes preferring this world's life; Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin, a direct choice against near pleasure.

The commentary says what follows is better than the first gain; Hebrews says Moses valued reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looked toward the reward, making future recompense govern present choice.
The commentary says the message is in former scrolls and names Moses; Jesus says Moses wrote about him, a New Testament interpretation that gives Mosaic scripture a forward-looking witness.

row.basis: losing present life to keep eternal life
row.note: The commentary says people prefer worldly life over the better later one; Jesus says one who loves life loses it, while one who gives up life in this world keeps it for eternal life, directly reversing that preference.

row.basis: prayer begins by hallowing the Father's name
row.note: The commentary says the worshipper remembers the Lord's name and then prays; Jesus teaches prayer that opens by asking that the Father's name be hallowed, joining divine-name devotion to the prayer itself.

row.basis: last and first at the kingdom's table
row.note: The commentary says the first arrival is not necessarily the winner; after describing entry into God's kingdom, Jesus says some who are last will be first and first last, placing the reversal in an eschatological gathering.
The commentary's horse holds strength for the latter stretch; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, making final persistence decisive.

The commentary says an early position does not guarantee the final win; Paul disciplines his body lest, after preaching to others, he himself be disqualified, adding the possibility that even a runner can fail at the end.

row.basis: athlete crowned only under the rules
row.note: The commentary links the race order to a later prize; Paul says an athlete is not crowned unless competing lawfully, adding that position and desire alone do not secure the outcome.

row.basis: rich urged not to hope in uncertain wealth
row.note: The commentary says people prefer worldly life; Paul tells the rich not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God, a specific correction to misplaced present security.

row.basis: treasure stored for the future life
row.note: The commentary calls the later life better and lasting; Paul says the rich should store up treasure as a foundation for the future and take hold of the life that is truly life, spelling out present action for future gain.
The commentary says the horse preserves its running for later; James blesses the one who endures trial and promises the crown of life, making the reward follow sustained endurance.
The commentary says the afterlife is more enduring; Peter describes an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven, adding a reserved future possession.

The commentary treats this life as an earlier position before the lasting life; Diognetus describes Christians as dwelling on earth while their citizenship is in heaven, giving the temporal contrast the image of temporary residence versus permanent homeland.
